BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Thursday as upper flow backs from westerly to southwesterly ahead of the next deep upper low off the WA coast. Showers developing Thursday night as the low comes inland.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A cold front with scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms will move east of the area early this evening.
- Showers continue in the mountains tonight through early Tuesday with a light dusting of snow expected above 6000 feet elevation.
- Gradual clearing by late Tuesday with temperatures several degrees below normal in the cooler air behind the front through Wednesday.
- Next best chance of widespread precipitation this weekend.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: isolated thunderstorms along a cold front moving west to east through southwestern Idaho will taper off early this evening in most areas. However shower activity will continue in the central Idaho mountains tonight, Snow levels will lower behind the front and a light dusting of snow will occur in the mountains above 6000 feet by Tuesday morning. Gradual clearing will occur on Tuesday with temperatures expected to be be a few degrees below normal in the cooler air behind the front through Wednesday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday as upper flow backs from westerly to southwesterly ahead of the next deep upper low off the WA coast. Showers developing Thursday night as the low comes inland. Surface cold front and widespread showers in western ID Friday, along with lowering snow level. Partial clearing and colder Friday night, then rain and snow showers again Saturday as the upper low comes in. Clearing, windy, and cold Monday under strong northwest flow aloft behind the eastward-exiting upper low.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A larger trough along with a possible subtropical moisture connection/jet off the central and eastern Pacific reaches the far southwest U.S. by late Saturday and Sunday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog, some dense, across the plains and I-25 Corridor tonight into Tuesday morning.
- Warmer and mostly dry much of this week.
- Unsettled weather potentially returning late in the weekend and early next week, with a 20-30% chance of season's first snow in lower elevations toward Tuesday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The upper level trough that brought the overnight/early morning rain and mountain snow is pushing well to our northeast, with drier and more subsident airmass building in behind it. However, abundant low level moisture remained in place east of the Front Range, with the stratus deck only slowly burning off. While we do expect more clearing through the late afternoon hours, areas of low clouds and fog will redevelop tonight in the moist boundary layer. This will be a hybrid radiational/advection fog event, with contributions from a developing weak Denver Cyclone. The expected location of the cyclone developing near/south of metro Denver and pushing slowly northeast overnight into early Tuesday morning favors fog over the eastern and northern plains, but then also wrapping around the back side of the cyclone down the I-25 Corridor into at least the northern suburbs by/shortly after midnight. There's a 50-60% chance it moves as far south as the southern Denver suburbs before daybreak. Given the hybrid event and relatively narrow T/Td spreads, we think some areas will experience dense fog. It's quite difficult to narrow the exact locations of thickest fog development, but something to watch for the overnight and early morning hours with potential for a Dense Fog Advisory. We'll continue to monitor through the evening and overnight.

On Tuesday, we're not sure that we'll see the magnitude of warming we earlier anticipated. That's because of the morning stratus and fog, and lack of lee troughing. We've generally cut temperatures a few degrees across the lower elevations but still mostly lower to mid 60s for highs (but a 30-40% chance we only hit the mid to upper 50s over the eastern plains). What we are more certain about is that tomorrow will start a 3-4 day stretch of dry weather.

That dry weather will be courtesy of drier and brisk west to southwest flow aloft. There will be warm advection and flat ridging by Thursday, which should support highs pushing to near 70F across the plains and I-25 Corridor.

Ensembles are still showing a subtropical push or partial remnants (or at least water vapor transport) of Tropical Storm Vance in the eastern tropical Pacific getting drawn up as early as Friday. However, the main impacts of this would very likely (>80%) chance stay to the east of our forecast area. We'll only have a slight chance of showers reaching the far eastern plains by late Friday.

A larger trough along with a possible subtropical moisture connection/jet off the central and eastern Pacific reaches the far southwest U.S. by late Saturday and Sunday. While that is fairly well agreed upon by ensemble systems, models diverge significantly by the time we reach Sunday into early next week. Yes, there is general troughiness and storminess expected, but some models move the trough through as an open or even shearing wave, while others develop a deep closed low somewhere between the Midwest and Colorado. It was interesting to note the EPS showed a rather marked increase in precipitation and even snow potential as we head toward Tuesday of next week, while the GEFS showed no discernible trend. The EPS had close to 30% of the members showing snow for Denver and the plains, while GEFS supported much lower odds (10-20%). Some of these runs, of course, were much colder than the vast majority of the ensembles, as evidenced in the large temperature variations (25th-75th percentiles from highs in the mid 40s to mid 60s for Monday and Tuesday, but full range of outcomes from highs in the upper 20s to lower 70s). Stay tuned for the latest trends and what could maybe, just maybe, be our first snowfall in the lower elevations should the deeper/slower solutions verify.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Deterministic models are in better agreement for next weekend, but ensembles still depict relatively low confidence with precipitation chances...mainly due to the evolution and speed of the Pacific energy moving onshore.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread rain showers and mountain snowfall expected through Monday morning as a central Pacific system lifts northeast across the region.
- Near normal temperatures and a bit warmer by Tuesday through Thursday, but the next Pacific system will be approaching from the eastern Pacific later in the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Well that was a fun start to the day for the Nebraska Panhandle. Basically as the low pressure system was wrapping up and pushing North-northeast a little band of FGEN (area of enhanced rain/snowfall) set up over the southern panhandle that no model was tracking correctly. Due to the band of enhanced rainfall the temperatures dropped and the rain transitioned to snowfall a lot faster than anticipated. A last minute SPS was issued for the Western portion of the Panhandle for localized 1-3 inches that may cause some possible delays. There was a report of 3 inches on the border of the Banner and Scotts Bluff county to confirm the SPS was needed. Mid-level water vapor showed dry air eventually being ingested by the Low pressure system eventually causing the showers to slowly dissipate in the southern half of the Panhandle. Dawes county is currently the last county with active snow showers but those should eventually stop around 3pm-ish. However, with all this low level moisture and an area of high pressure following in the systems wake, the cloud cover may resurface overnight for the Panhandle and the far eastern side of the SOutheast Wyoming area. This overnight cloud cover though will keep us relatively warmer overnight with temperatures in the mid to upper 30's with some areas reaching around 40 degrees. Another system is making landfall over the pacific northwest which will compress the gradient as it runs into our area of high pressure. Meaning tomorrow morning it will be fairly windy west of the I-25 corridor between Rawlins and Laramie as the 700mb jet creeps up to speeds around 55 knots and diurnal mixing starts to occur. Wind gusts up to 60 mph may be likely along that wind prone stretch of I-80 but wind gusts between 50 to 55 mph may be more likely. These gusty winds will taper down from those elevated gusts through the afternoon but it will be fairly breezy through the overnight hours. Temperatures are expected to be in the 50's and 60's by Tuesday afternoon but the mountain peaks will stay closer to the mid 30's during the afternoon hours. The models have some overnight clouds pushing through Tuesday night as that system from the Pacific Northwest climbs back into the Canadian providences as it goes up and over our area of developing high pressure. If any clouds remain over our forecast area overnight then the spots underneath those clouds may be a touch warmer that forecasted.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Medium Range models remain in good agreement for much of mid to late week as weak to moderate southwest flow aloft dominates the weather pattern across the northern Front Range. With a lack of Pacific (shortwave) energy embedded in the mean southwest flow aloft through Friday, expect generally dry conditions and mild temperatures Wednesday through Friday as the polar jet stream will remain well to the north, and the subtropical jet should stay well south of the region near the Mexico/USA border and into Texas. Since southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska will be in between storm tracks, relatively mild temperatures are expected through the end of the week with afternoon highs in the upper 50s to upper 60s. Temperatures should peak Friday afternoon as 700mb temperatures climb over 5c ahead of the next Pacific storm system moving onshore, with a few locations possibly reaching 70 degrees east of the Interstate 25 corridor.

Deterministic models are in better agreement for next weekend, but ensembles still depict relatively low confidence with precipitation chances...mainly due to the evolution and speed of the Pacific energy moving onshore. Thankfully, with the Pacific energy trending a little slower, Halloween evening looks decent with maybe a few rain showers in the evening. Temperatures should be relatively mild for this time of the year in the upper 30s to upper 40s between sunset and 10:00 PM. Winds appear light and variable and should result in a pleasant evening. Models do show the first of a series of upper level disturbances lifting northward across the area on Halloween, but the system is pretty progressive with the best dynamics located north and west of the I-25 corridor. A more potent system is forecast to arrive on Sunday and continue early next week. Model solutions and ensemble members diverge significantly with this storm system, so will not go into too much detail at this time. However, temperatures will trend cooler and likely below average for this time of the year by next Sunday and Monday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Late Thursday, models begin to develop a system that drops southward down the PACNW coast. Presently, this system digs southward Friday and Saturday. This will ramp up southwesterly flow across the Four Corners.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flooding and high flows along the San Juan river continue for southeast Utah into Tuesday.
- Monday through Thursday is expected to be mostly dry, but another impactful system is possible next weekend.
- Model guidance reflects some uncertainty in storm tracks, leading to inconsistencies in moisture volume forecasts.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Warmer and drier conditions have begun to develop across the West Slope today, as weak higher pressure invades. Temperatures will inch up toward average values by week's end. The dry conditions will help with flood waters that have begun to recede across southern CO and southeast UT. A weak clipper system working across the PACNW on Tuesday will bring a few clouds to northwest CO. Non zero precipitation chances could bring an isolated sprinkle or flurry to the high country up there, but little to no measurable moisture is expected.

Late Thursday, models begin to develop a system that drops southward down the PACNW coast. Presently, this system digs southward Friday and Saturday. This will ramp up southwesterly flow across the Four Corners. Winds will likely pick up in the forecasts as the week progresses and models get a better handle on this system. Storm tracks and depth of cold air are an early point of concern in this forecast. Model runs have already pushed impacts further out than initial runs were projecting. Probabilistic guidance is still indicating 50/50 chances for heavier rainfall across southwest CO Sunday and Monday. Saturated soils from this weekend's storms make this a much more impactful forecast, as low end rainfall totals could push streams back towards action stage. For now, the strongest moisture push arrives Sunday into Monday. Snow levels remain around 10000 feet, which is very similar to the last storm, leaving the bulk of lower elevations in rainfall. This is a developing forecast and will become more refined as details emerge from the models, giving more clarity.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Friday through Sunday...Broad Pacific trough, with a low center just off the Pacific NW coast, will start to strengthen and drop south along the coastline Thu, which will by Fri produce deep southwest flow across the Desert Sw and the Four Corners.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Warm and dry through Thursday, then a pattern shift starting Friday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Just a quick update to adjust pops across Baca County and fog potential overnight for the San Luis Valley, lower Arkansas River Valley and up near the Palmer Divide. A few showers will remain possible through midnight across Baca County as an upper system pulls away from the area. Fog is forecast to develop overnight into Tuesday morning, with visibility reducing to near 1 mile at times.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Remnants of the upper low pressure system were gradually sliding northeast out of the area, providing for mostly sunny skies to develop over the western portions of the county warning area. However, a good amount of cloudiness remained across the southeast corner of the state. Temps as of 1 PM have warmed into the 40s to around 50F for the high valleys, and 50s to lower 60s for the plains.

Tonight through Tuesday...As the upper disturbance leaves the region, and another shortwave crosses the northern Rockies, somewhat light west to southwest flow aloft will develop across the state and the Four Corners region. A few lingering showers are expected across Baca County this evening, otherwise dry conditions are anticipated. The disturbance passing by to the north will tighten the pressure gradient enough for some afternoon gustiness tomorrow across the higher terrain and foothills, but for the most part plan on a mild and pleasant day with warmer temperatures. Mostly clear skies tonight will lead to efficient radiational cooling, with the chance for another shot at patchy fog during the overnight and early morning hours, especially across the San Luis Valley and the Arkansas River Valley.

Look for overnight lows in the 20s to around 30F for the high valleys, and 30s to around 40F for the plains. High temps Tuesday will climb into the mid 50s to lower 60s for the high valleys, and 60s to around 70F for the plains.

Ongoing high flows across the Rio Grande and Conejos Rivers will continue for at least another few days. Conditions should be closely monitored for ongoing impacts. In addition, high flow is currently moving down the Purgatoire River from recent rainfall, and is expected to produce some minor flooding near Las Animas late tonight which will last through Tuesday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Wednesday and Thursday...West-southwest flow continues across the region through mid week, providing for dry conditions and warm temps, with highs on Wednesday 5-10 degrees above normal. Another fast-moving shortwave crossing the Rockies Wed will push a weak cold front south into eastern CO early Thu, dropping afternoon highs Thu by about 5 degrees.

Friday through Sunday...Broad Pacific trough, with a low center just off the Pacific NW coast, will start to strengthen and drop south along the coastline Thu, which will by Fri produce deep southwest flow across the Desert Sw and the Four Corners. This will once again draw moisture up into the western half of the state, leading to cooler and more active weather into the weekend, as well as accumulating mt snow starting Fri night. There are some variations in the long range solutions between models, so this is a little early getting into specifics. Moore

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Cooler air moving in with the aforementioned trough on Sunday will result in snow levels dipping around 8000-8500 feet. As such, accumulating snowfall is expected for all Utah mountains into Monday morning.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A couple of weak systems brushing northern Utah through mid-week will keep temperatures seasonably cool, with mostly dry conditions prevailing.
- Two storm systems bring wetter weather back to the region Friday into the weekend, with widespread precipitation through this period resulting in an increased risk for flash flooding.
- Colder air moving in Saturday into early Monday will result in lowering snow levels, allowing for accumulating snowfall generally above 8500 feet.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Generally benign conditions are expected for the first half of this week. While a couple weak systems are expected to brush northern Utah through mid-week -- the first moving through overnight tonight, and the second late Tuesday into Wednesday -- little impact is expected outside of a slight cooldown and some isolated showers near the Idaho border.

A more active pattern is expected late this week into the weekend as a couple stronger weather systems with more efficient moisture taps impact the region. The first system arrives Friday as a shortwave ejects around the eastern periphery of a deepening trough along the west coast. Increasing southerly flow aloft will bring an influx of tropical moisture to the region, with PWAT anomalies increasing to around 200-250% of normal across much of southern and central Utah on Friday into early Saturday. There is still quite a bit of spread on how much precipitation this system brings to the region, with the 25th percentile showing next to northing across much of Utah and southwest Wyoming, while the 75th percentile brings 0.3-0.5 inches to much of southern Utah except upwards of an inch across the southern mountains. Given recent rainfall across central and southern Utah, the flash flood risk is elevated Friday into Saturday despite this uncertainty. WPC currently highlights much of southern Utah under a Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 4) of excessive rainfall through this period.

Ensembles show good agreement on a brief lull on Saturday afternoon ahead of the second, more potent system. A strong atmospheric river is expected to make landfall along the southern California coast late Saturday, bringing a stream of very deep tropical moisture that will overspread much of Utah and southwest Wyoming on Sunday. Concurrently, an upper-level trough begins to dig southward into the Great Basin, resulting in substantial instability developing across the region. As such, ensembles are in good agreement on this portion of the storm bringing widespread moderate to heavy rainfall to the region. While heavy rain is likely across southern Utah, with a 75% chance to exceed 1" of rain across much of the area through Monday morning, models show quite a bit of spread in rainfall accumulations across central and northern Utah given some models indicate potential for a more southerly track of deepest moisture. Across these areas, the 25th percentile brings a widespread 0.2-0.5", while the 75th percentile indicates widespread accumulations of 1.0-1.5".

Cooler air moving in with the aforementioned trough on Sunday will result in snow levels dipping around 8000-8500 feet. As such, accumulating snowfall is expected for all Utah mountains into Monday morning. Current forecast indicates 3-6" of snow accumulations between Sunday and Monday morning for elevations above 8500 feet, with locally higher totals of 6-10" across the central and southern Utah mountains and the Uintas.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Heavy rain on Wednesday and Thursday triggered small wet avalanches in the west-Central and Southern Mountains, but this concern is waning as temperatures drop. The most likely place to trigger an avalanche is at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) in the Southern and west-Central Mountains on west, north, and east-facing slopes where new snow has been accumulating and a layer of mid-October snow persists. The Northern Mountains remain mostly bare.

This weekend, a new storm will deliver 4 to 8 inches of snow to the San Juan and Sangre de Cristo Mountains, creating fresh avalanche concerns on upper-elevation, wind-drifted slopes facing west, north, and east. Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
